title: Cafeteria & Restaurant Workers Union v. McElroy (1961)
shortTitle: Cafeteria & Restaurant Workers Union v. McElroy (1961)
summary: The commander of a military installation may summarily bar a civilian contractor's employee from the base for security reasons without notice or a hearing, because the interest affected is narrow and the government acts as proprietor of its own installation.
notes:
Key line: "The very nature of due process negates any concept of inflexible procedures universally applicable to every imaginable situation." (Stewart, J.)

Citation: 367 U.S. 886 (1961).

sections.Parties: The petitioners were Rachel Brawner, a short order cook, and Cafeteria and Restaurant Workers Union, Local 473, which represented the employees of the cafeteria where she worked. The respondents were the Secretary of Defense, Neil McElroy, Rear Admiral D. M. Tyree, Superintendent of the Naval Gun Factory in Washington, D.C., and Lieutenant Commander H. C. Williams, the installation's Security Officer, sued in their individual and official capacities. Brawner's actual employer, M & M Restaurants, Inc., operated the cafeteria under a contract with the Gun Factory's Board of Governors and was not a party.
sections.Material Facts: In 1956 Brawner had worked for more than six years as a short order cook at the cafeteria that M & M Restaurants ran on the premises of the Naval Gun Factory, a restricted installation that designed and produced naval ordnance, including highly classified weapons systems. Access required badges issued by the Security Officer, and section 5(b)(iii) of M & M's contract barred it from employing anyone on the premises who failed to meet the installation's security requirements as determined by that officer. On November 15, 1956, Brawner was required to surrender her badge after Lieutenant Commander Williams determined that she failed those requirements; Admiral Tyree approved, citing the contract clause. At the union's request M & M asked for a hearing, which Tyree refused as serving no useful purpose. Brawner was never told the grounds. M & M offered her a job at a suburban restaurant, which she declined as inconvenient. No one accused her of disloyalty.
sections.Procedural History: Brawner and the union sued in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia seeking, among other relief, an order compelling return of her badge so she could resume her job. The defendants moved for summary judgment on affidavits and exhibits; the motion was granted and the complaint dismissed. A three judge panel of the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reversed, one judge dissenting, but on rehearing en banc the court withdrew that opinion and affirmed the district court, four judges dissenting, 284 F.2d 173. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, 364 U.S. 813, because of an alleged conflict with Greene v. McElroy, 360 U.S. 474, and affirmed on June 19, 1961, by a vote of 5 to 4.
sections.Issue: Two questions were presented. First, whether the commanding officer of the Gun Factory was authorized, by explicit delegation from Congress or the President of the kind found wanting in Greene v. McElroy, to deny Brawner access to the installation in the summary way he did. Second, if he was so authorized, whether excluding her without telling her the specific grounds and without a hearing at which she could refute them deprived her of liberty or property without due process of law under the Fifth Amendment.
sections.Holding: The Court held that Admiral Tyree had explicit authority. Article 0734 of the Navy Regulations, approved by the President as the law required, provided that dealers or tradesmen or their agents shall not be admitted within a command except as authorized by the commanding officer, and this codified the historically unquestioned power of a commander to exclude civilians from a military base. The Court further held that the Due Process Clause was not violated. Brawner lost only the opportunity to work at one isolated military installation, the government acted as proprietor of its own internal affairs, the stated reason was rational and consistent with the contract, and no badge of disloyalty or infamy foreclosing other employment was imposed. The judgment was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Stewart accepted that the explicit authorization required by Greene had to be shown, and found it in Navy Regulations approved by President Truman on August 9, 1948, which the Court treated as endowed with the sanction of law. Attorney General opinions dating from 1837 and Judge Advocate General rulings confirmed that post commanders had always excluded tradesmen at will. On the constitutional question, the Court refused to dispose of the case by saying Brawner had no right to be there, quoting Homer v. Richmond on the right to go to Baghdad. Instead it explained that due process is not a fixed set of procedures and requires attention to the precise nature of the government function and the private interest affected. Brawner's interest was not the right to follow her trade, since she could work as a cook anywhere else; the function was proprietary management of a military installation, not regulation or licensing of a profession. Government employment, absent legislation, may be terminated at will, as In re Hennen and Vitarelli v. Seaton showed. United Public Workers and Wieman meant only that exclusion on patently arbitrary or discriminatory grounds would be unconstitutional, not that notice and hearing were required whenever the reason given was rational. Finally, nothing indicated that failing the security requirements of one installation branded Brawner as disloyal or impaired her employment elsewhere; she may simply have been garrulous or careless with her badge.

topics.lrs-o-new-property: Although Brawner lost, the Court rejected a categorical privilege answer and examined the governmental function and the precise affected interest.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 5 to 4. Justice Brennan dissented, joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justices Black and Douglas. He doubted that the exclusion was authorized but, accepting the Court's holding on authority, argued that the Court recognized a right not to be arbitrarily excluded and then gave it no procedural protection at all: Brawner was not told what she did wrong and had no chance to defend herself, so an official could use security requirements as a blind for discrimination. He added that the label security risk carries a sinister public meaning, so some statement of charges and opportunity to reply was required by fundamental fairness.
